planting.note: Start seedlings in a nursery bed and transplant 3-4 week old seedlings into warm, fertile lowland soil once all frost danger has passed; unlike many paddy rices, this landrace is traditionally grown on free-draining fields with a naturally high but not flooded water table rather than deep standing water.

directions: Ofada is a named landrace rice grown almost exclusively around the town of Ofada in Ogun State, southwestern Nigeria, and prized for the nutty, earthy aroma and firm, chewy bite that comes from leaving much of the bran intact during minimal milling. Grain color varies between batches, with unpolished brown or reddish seed (locally called ofada pupa) tending toward strongly aromatic, while the paler white form (ofada funfun) is typically milder. Rather than standing floodwater, this landrace is traditionally cultivated on free-draining fields where the water table stays close to but below the root zone, so plan for consistently moist, well-irrigated soil rather than a deep flooded paddy. The variety is valued by smallholders for its tolerance of local pests and its adaptability to south-west Nigeria's rain-fed lowland conditions, and the grain is the traditional base for the iconic Nigerian ayamase (designer) pepper stew.
sources: Nigerian Food Journal — Physical and Pasting Properties of 'Ofada' Rice (Oryza sativa L.) Varieties
Ofada Rice Identity, Physical Qualities and Processing Technology Options for Upgrading: A Review

common_name: NERICA-4 Rice (Upland New Rice for Africa)

planting.note: Direct sow in warm, well-drained upland soil once frost danger has passed; this is a dryland rice bred for rain-fed fields and does not need flooding like traditional lowland paddy rice.

directions: NERICA-4 is an interspecific hybrid between Asian rice (Oryza sativa) and African rice (Oryza glaberrima) developed by the Africa Rice Center (WARDA) to combine the yield potential of Asian rice with the rusticity of its African parent. It became the most widely grown of the upland NERICA line, adopted across more than ten sub-Saharan African countries including Nigeria and Ghana, largely because of its strong tolerance to drought and low soil phosphorus, two of the biggest constraints facing rain-fed upland rice farmers. Plants grow to roughly waist height and produce bold, aromatic grain with good milling quality and moderate resistance to rice blast, maturing quickly enough to fit shorter rainy seasons than many older varieties. Grow it as a dryland crop in full sun with consistently moist but not flooded soil, direct-seeding once the soil has warmed and weeding early since the upright but modest canopy competes poorly with weeds in its first weeks.

planting.note: Plant a sucker (sword sucker or pup) after frost danger has passed in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake the pseudostem once the heavy bunch begins to fill out.

directions: Agbagba is a long-cultivated False Horn plantain landrace of the Musa AAB group and one of the most widely grown and preferred plantain cultivars across Nigeria, favored by many households for its cooking and eating qualities even though newer IITA-bred hybrids now out-yield it substantially. In side-by-side trials it has shown markedly lower resistance to black Sigatoka leaf disease than modern hybrid lines and produces noticeably smaller bunches, yet it remains a benchmark variety that breeders use for comparison when evaluating new plantain releases for Nigerian farmers. Grow it from a sucker planted in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, watering and feeding heavily through the growing season since plantains are gross feeders, and stake the pseudostem as the bunch fills to prevent toppling in wind. Watch for black Sigatoka and burrowing nematodes, both of which affect this older landrace more than disease-screened modern hybrids.
sources: International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) — plantain and banana breeding research

common_name: Apantu Plantain (Ghana's Leading False Horn Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant a sucker after frost danger has passed in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake the pseudostem as the bunch develops since fruit is heavy.

directions: Apantu, sometimes called Apantu pa, is a False Horn plantain of the Musa AAB group and the most widely grown and preferred plantain cultivar in Ghana, cultivated alongside the French-type Apem cultivar but generally favored by farmers and processors for giving a notably higher pulp-to-peel ratio, meaning more usable flesh per fruit. That trait makes it a popular choice for the boiled, roasted, and fried plantain dishes central to Ghanaian cuisine as well as for flour and chip processing. Propagate from a sucker set in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, watering and feeding generously since plantains are heavy feeders, and stake the pseudostem as the bunch fills out to prevent the plant from toppling. As with other West African plantain landraces, watch for black Sigatoka leaf spot and nematodes, which can shorten the productive life of a stand over successive cycles.
